midnat.explanation: "Midnat" means "midnight". Do not mix it up with "middag" (dinner). To say what time you eat dinner, use it for the meal: "Vi spiser middag klokken seks" (We eat dinner at six).

midt.explanation: "Midt" means "in the middle". To say where the middle of a place is, use "midt i" (in the middle of): "midt i byen" (in the middle of town). To say the middle of a part of the day, use "midt på" (in the middle of): "midt på dagen" (in the middle of the day).

mig.explanation: "Mig" means "me". When you are the one doing the action, use "jeg" (I) instead: "Jeg ser ham" (I see him). When you do something to yourself, "mig" means "myself": "Jeg vasker mig" (I wash myself). After "til" (to) and "med" (with), use "mig" too: "til mig" (to me), "med mig" (with me).

mild.explanation: "Mild" means "mild". To talk about the weather, use it for a season: "Vinteren er mild i år" (The winter is mild this year). To talk about food that is not strong, use it for a food: "en mild ost" (a mild cheese).

militær.explanation: "Militær" means "military". When you talk about the armed forces as a whole, add "-et" to make the noun: "militæret" (the military). To say someone serves in them: "Han er i militæret" (He is in the military).

million.explanation: "En million" means "a million". English never adds an ending to "million" after a number, but Danish does. To say two million, use: "to millioner mennesker" (two million people). Do not mix it up with "en milliard" (a billion, which is 1,000 million). To say how much money, use: "en milliard kroner" (a billion kroner).

min.explanation: "Min" means "my". To say my car, use it with one car: "min bil" (my car). With one house, use "mit" instead: "mit hus" (my house). With more than one thing, use "mine": "mine børn" (my children).

related.en: your (with one thing like a car)

mindre.explanation: "Mindre" means "less". When you describe the size of a thing, it means "smaller": "et mindre hus" (a smaller house). Do not mix it up with "mindst" (least): "Hun har mindst penge" (She has the least money).

mindst.explanation: "Mindst" means "least". To ask who has the smallest amount of something, use it before the thing: "Hvem har mindst tid?" (Who has the least time?) To give the lowest number that is fine, use it before a number, where it means "at least": "mindst fem" (at least five).

mine.explanation: "Mine" means "my". When you talk about more than one thing, use it: "mine huse" (my houses). With one house, use "mit" instead: "mit hus" (my house). With one book, use "min" instead: "min bog" (my book).

minigolf.explanation: "Minigolf" means "mini golf". Unlike the English spelling, Danish has no space inside "minigolf".

minimal.explanation: "Minimal" means "minimal". Its opposite is "maksimal" (maximum). To say the highest speed that is possible, use the opposite: "maksimal hastighed" (maximum speed).

misfornøjet.explanation: "Misfornøjet" means "dissatisfied". It is built from "mis-" and "fornøjet" (pleased). The start "mis-" also works like English "mis-" in "at misforstå" (to misunderstand).

misforstået.explanation: "Misforstået" means "misunderstood". It comes from the verb "at misforstå" (to misunderstand). To call a feeling or loyalty misguided, use it too: "misforstået loyalitet" (misguided loyalty).

misinformation.explanation: "Misinformation" means "misinformation". Do not mix it up with "desinformation" (disinformation). Misinformation is false information spread by mistake: "Det er misinformation" (That is misinformation). Disinformation is false information spread on purpose: "Det er desinformation" (That is disinformation).

mistillid.explanation: "En mistillid" means "distrust". It is built from "mis-" and "tillid" (trust). To talk about a vote of no confidence in a government, use "et mistillidsvotum": "Der er et mistillidsvotum mod regeringen" (There is a vote of no confidence against the government).

mistænkelig.explanation: "Mistænkelig" means "suspicious". Do not mix it up with "mistænksom" (suspicious of others). To say a thing seems wrong, use "mistænkelig": "en mistænkelig lyd" (a suspicious sound). To say a person does not trust others, use "mistænksom": "en mistænksom nabo" (a neighbor who distrusts others).

mistænksom.explanation: "Mistænksom" means "suspicious". Do not mix it up with "mistænkelig" (looking suspicious). To say a person does not trust others, use "mistænksom": "en mistænksom nabo" (a neighbor who distrusts others). To say a thing seems wrong, use "mistænkelig": "en mistænkelig lyd" (a suspicious sound).

mistænkt.explanation: "Mistænkt" means "suspected". To name the person the police are looking at, use the noun "en mistænkt" (a suspect): "Politiet har en mistænkt" (The police have a suspect).

misundelig.explanation: "Misundelig" means "envious". To say who you envy, add "på" (of): "Han er misundelig på sin kollega" (He is envious of his coworker).

misundelse.explanation: "En misundelse" means "envy". Do not mix it up with "jalousi" (jealousy), the fear of losing a partner to someone else. To talk about that fear, say: "Jalousi kan ødelægge et forhold" (Jealousy can ruin a relationship).

misvisende.explanation: "Misvisende" means "misleading". The start "mis-" also appears in "at misforstå" (to misunderstand) and "mistillid" (distrust).

mit.explanation: "Mit" means "my". Use it with one thing that takes "et", as in "mit værelse" (my room). With one car, use "min" instead: "min bil" (my car). With more than one thing, use "mine": "mine børn" (my children).

related.en: your (with one thing like a room)

mod.explanation: "Mod" means "toward". To point to a direction, use it before the place: "Han går mod døren" (He walks toward the door). When you play an opponent, it means "against": "Danmark spiller mod Norge" (Denmark plays against Norway). To say you are against an idea, use "imod" (against) instead: "Jeg er imod det" (I am against it).

mode.explanation: "Mode" means "fashion". Do not mix it up with "en måde" (a way). To say a good way to learn, say: "Det er en god måde at lære på" (That is a good way to learn).

moderigtig.explanation: "Moderigtig" means "fashionable". It is built from "mode" (fashion) and "rigtig" (right), so it is literally "right for the fashion".

moderne.explanation: "Moderne" means "modern". To say something is not modern, use the opposite, "gammeldags" (old-fashioned): "et gammeldags køkken" (an old-fashioned kitchen).

modgang.explanation: "En modgang" means "adversity". Its opposite is "medgang" (good fortune). To say through good times and bad, use both words together: "i medgang og modgang" (in good times and bad).

modig.explanation: "Modig" means "brave". It comes from "mod" (courage). To say you are scared instead, use "bange" (scared): "Jeg er bange for edderkopper" (I am scared of spiders).

modløs.explanation: "Modløs" means "discouraged". It is built from "mod" (courage) and "-løs" (without), so it is literally "without courage".

modsat.explanation: "Modsat" means "opposite". To name the opposite thing itself, say "det modsatte": "Det modsatte af varm er kold" (The opposite of hot is cold).

modstandsdygtig.explanation: "Modstandsdygtig" means "resilient". It is built from "modstand" (resistance) and "dygtig" (skilled).

moms.explanation: "Moms" means "VAT". To ask whether the price includes VAT, say: "Er det med moms?" (Is VAT included?)

moralsk.explanation: "Moralsk" means "moral". To say you are bound by what is right, use it with "pligt" (duty): "en moralsk pligt" (a moral duty).

morgenmad.explanation: "Morgenmad" means "breakfast". It is built from "morgen" (morning) and "mad" (food). When you mean breakfast in general, leave out "en": "Jeg spiser morgenmad" (I eat breakfast).

morsom.explanation: "Morsom" means "amusing". To say a story makes you smile, use it: "en morsom historie" (an amusing story). Do not mix it up with "sjov" (fun, funny): "Festen var sjov" (The party was fun).

mos.explanation: "Et mos" means "moss / mash". To talk about the green plant on a roof, say: "Der er mos på taget" (There is moss on the roof). To talk about mashed potatoes, put "kartoffel" (potato) in front: "Jeg laver kartoffelmos" (I am making mashed potatoes).

motion.explanation: "Motion" means "exercise", as in physical activity. For an exercise in a lesson, use "en øvelse" (an exercise): "en øvelse i grammatik" (a grammar exercise).

motivation.explanation: "Motivation" means "motivation". It is the noun for the verb "at motivere" (to motivate).

mozzarella.explanation: "Mozzarella" means "mozzarella". To say what a pizza has on it, use "med" (with): "pizza med mozzarella" (pizza with mozzarella).

mudder.explanation: "Et mudder" means "mud". To say you are stuck in it, use "fast i" (stuck in): "Bilen sidder fast i mudderet" (The car is stuck in the mud).

mulig.explanation: "Mulig" means "possible". To ask someone to hurry, use the set phrase "så hurtigt som muligt" (as fast as possible): "Kom så hurtigt som muligt" (Come as fast as possible).

muligvis.explanation: "Muligvis" means "possibly". It is built from "mulig" (possible). To answer a question with one word, say: "Kommer hun?" "Muligvis." (Is she coming? Possibly.)

mundtlig.explanation: "Mundtlig" means "oral". It comes from "en mund" (a mouth), so it is literally "of the mouth". To say an exam is done in writing, use the opposite, "skriftlig" (written): "en skriftlig eksamen" (a written exam).

munter.explanation: "Munter" means "cheerful". To describe a tune that sounds happy, use it too: "en munter melodi" (a cheerful tune).

musik.explanation: "Musik" means "music". This word has no article when it means music in general, so leave out "en": "Jeg elsker musik" (I love music). To say a school lesson is music, use "at have" (to have): "Vi har musik i dag" (We have music today).

musikalsk.explanation: "Musikalsk" means "musical". It comes from the noun "musik" (music). To describe a whole family, use it too: "en musikalsk familie" (a musical family).

muskuløs.explanation: "Muskuløs" means "muscular". It comes from "en muskel" (a muscle). Do not mix it up with "stærk" (strong). To say a man has power but not big muscles, say: "Han er stærk, men ikke muskuløs" (He is strong, but not muscular).

muslimsk.explanation: "Muslimsk" means "Muslim". To name a person, use the noun "en muslim" (a Muslim): "Min nabo er muslim" (My neighbor is a Muslim). To describe a custom or a prayer, use "muslimsk": "en muslimsk bøn" (a Muslim prayer).

mystisk.explanation: "Mystisk" means "mysterious". To describe a sound at night that you cannot explain, use it: "en mystisk lyd om natten" (a mysterious sound at night). Do not mix it up with "mærkelig" (strange). To describe something that is only odd, use "mærkelig": "en mærkelig hat" (a strange hat).

mytologi.explanation: "En mytologi" means "a mythology". To name the old stories of one people, put the people before it: "den græske mytologi" (Greek mythology).

må jeg bede om regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg bede om regningen?" means "May I have the bill?". Literally, "bede om" means "ask for", so it asks "May I ask for the bill?". To ask for something else, keep the start and change the end: "Må jeg bede om et glas vand?" (May I have a glass of water?)

må jeg få regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg få regningen?" means "May I have the bill?". Literally, "få" means "get", so it asks "May I get the bill?". To ask for something else, keep the start and change the end: "Må jeg få et glas vand?" (May I have a glass of water?)

målrettet.explanation: "Målrettet" means "goal-oriented". It is built from "et mål" (a goal) and "rettet" (aimed).

månedsvis.explanation: "Månedsvis" means "months", as in lasting for months. It is built from "en måned" (a month) and the ending "-vis". To say how long you waited, put it after the verb: "Vi har ventet månedsvis" (We have waited for months).

måske.explanation: "Måske" means "maybe". To answer a question when you are not sure, say: "Kommer du?" "Måske." (Are you coming? Maybe.)

mægtig.explanation: "Mægtig" means "mighty". It comes from "en magt" (a power). To say a tree is huge and impressive, use it: "et mægtigt træ" (a mighty tree).

mælk.explanation: "Mælk" means "milk". To say how much milk, use a measure first: "en liter mælk" (a liter of milk).

mærkbar.explanation: "Mærkbar" means "noticeable". It is built from "at mærke" (to feel) and "-bar" (able to be). Do not mix it up with "mærkelig" (strange): "en mærkelig lyd" (a strange sound).

mærkelig.explanation: "Mærkelig" means "strange". It comes from "at mærke" (to notice). Do not mix it up with "mærkbar" (noticeable): "en mærkbar forskel" (a noticeable difference).

mæt.explanation: "Mæt" means "full", as in having eaten enough. To say you have eaten enough, say: "Jeg er mæt" (I am full). After a meal, do not say "Jeg er fuld", because "fuld" means "drunk".

mættende.explanation: "Mættende" means "filling". It comes from the verb "at mætte" (to fill up). Do not mix it up with "mæt" (full), which describes a person: "Jeg er mæt" (I am full). "Mættende" describes food: "en mættende suppe" (a filling soup).

møbleret.explanation: "Møbleret" means "furnished". It comes from the verb "at møblere" (to furnish). To say a place has no furniture, add "u-": "en umøbleret lejlighed" (an unfurnished apartment).

mør.explanation: "Mør" means "tender". To say meat is hard to chew, use the opposite, "sej" (tough): "Kødet er sejt" (The meat is tough). In "en mørbrad" (a tenderloin), the part "mør" means "tender".

mørk.explanation: "Mørk" means "dark". In color names, the form "mørke-" (dark) goes first: "mørkeblå" (dark blue).

mørke.explanation: "Mørke" means "darkness". Do not mix it up with "mørk" (dark). To describe a room without light, use "mørk": "et mørkt rum" (a dark room).

mørkeblå.explanation: "Mørkeblå" means "dark blue". It is built from "mørk" (dark) and "blå" (blue). To say a blue is bright like a clear sky, use "himmelblå" (sky blue): "en himmelblå trøje" (a sky-blue sweater).

mørkegrøn.explanation: "Mørkegrøn" means "dark green". It is built from "mørk" (dark) and "grøn" (green). To say a green is fresh like grass, use "græsgrøn" (grass green): "en græsgrøn plæne" (a grass-green lawn).

mørketid.explanation: "En mørketid" means "a dark season". It is built from "mørke" (darkness) and "tid" (time).

mørkhåret.explanation: "Mørkhåret" means "dark-haired". It is built from "mørk" (dark), "hår" (hair) and the ending "-et". To say someone has blue eyes, the same pattern works: "en blåøjet pige" (a blue-eyed girl).

müsli.explanation: "Müsli" means "muesli". Danish spells it with "ü" and no "e", unlike the English spelling.

at narre.explanation: "At narre" means "to fool / trick". To say someone tricked you, say: "Hun narrede os alle" (She fooled us all). Do not mix it up with "at snyde" (to cheat): "Han snyder i kortspil" (He cheats at cards).

at navngive.explanation: "At navngive" means "to name", as in giving something a name. It is built from "et navn" (a name) and "at give" (to give). To say what someone is called, use "at hedde" (to be called): "Hun hedder Anna" (Her name is Anna).

at nedbryde.explanation: "At nedbryde" means "to break down", as in splitting into smaller parts. It is built from "ned" (down) and "at bryde" (to break). To say living things split waste into smaller parts, say: "Bakterier nedbryder affald" (Bacteria break down waste). To say you remove an obstacle, use it too: "at nedbryde barrierer" (to break down barriers).

at nedkæmpe.explanation: "At nedkæmpe" means "to defeat / suppress". It is built from "ned" (down) and "at kæmpe" (to fight). To say soldiers put down a rebellion, say: "Soldaterne nedkæmper oprøret" (The soldiers put down the rebellion).

at nedlægge.explanation: "At nedlægge" means "to shut down / lay down". It is built from "ned" (down) and "at lægge" (to lay). To say a service is closed for good, say: "nedlægge en buslinje" (shut down a bus line). To say you place flowers in memory of someone, say: "nedlægge en krans" (lay a wreath).

at nedsætte.explanation: "At nedsætte" means "to reduce". It is built from "ned" (down) and "at sætte" (to put). To say you drive more slowly, say: "nedsætte farten" (reduce speed). When you form a new group, it means "to set up": "nedsætte en arbejdsgruppe" (set up a working group).

at nedtone.explanation: "At nedtone" means "to downplay". It is built from "ned" (down) and "tone" (tone), like turning the volume down. To say someone made a problem sound small, say: "Chefen nedtonede problemet" (The boss downplayed the problem).

at nikke.explanation: "At nikke" means "to nod". To say someone shook their head, use "at ryste på hovedet" (to shake your head): "Han rystede på hovedet" (He shook his head).

at nippe.explanation: "At nippe" means "to sip". To say what you sip, add "til" (to) before it: "nippe til teen" (sip the tea).

at notere.explanation: "At notere" means "to note down". It comes from "en note" (a note).

at nusse.explanation: "At nusse" means "to cuddle / stroke". Do not mix it up with "at kramme" (to hug). To say you squeeze someone in your arms, use "at kramme": "Jeg krammer min mormor" (I hug my grandmother).

at nyde.explanation: "At nyde" means "to enjoy". To say you enjoy a meal, put the meal after the verb: "Vi nyder middagen" (We are enjoying the dinner).

at nyse.explanation: "At nyse" means "to sneeze". The noun for one sneeze is "et nys": "Der kom et højt nys" (There came a loud sneeze).

at nytte.explanation: "At nytte" means "to be of use". To say something is no use, add "ikke" (not): "Det nytter ikke" (It is no use). To ask whether something helps, say: "Nytter det noget?" (Does it do any good?)

at nå.explanation: "At nå" means "to reach / make it". To say you got somewhere, use the place after it: "Vi nåede hjem" (We got home). To say you were not in time, add "det" (it): "Jeg nåede det ikke" (I did not make it).

at nå det.explanation: "At nå det" means "to make it". To ask whether you will be in time, say: "Tror du, vi når det?" (Do you think we will make it?) When you name the thing you reach, leave out "det" (it): "Jeg nåede bussen" (I caught the bus).

at nå toget.explanation: "At nå toget" means "to catch the train". It is "at nå" (to reach) with "toget" (the train). To say you were too late, add "ikke" (not) after the verb: "Jeg nåede ikke toget" (I missed the train).

at nægte.explanation: "At nægte" means "to refuse". To say someone will not do something, add "at" (to) and the action: "Han nægter at komme" (He refuses to come). When someone says a thing is not true, it means "to deny": "Hun nægter, at hun tog den" (She denies that she took it).

at nærme sig.explanation: "At nærme sig" means "to approach". It comes from "nær" (close). To say you come closer to a place, name the place after the verb: "Vi nærmer os byen" (We are approaching the city). To say a date is coming, use it for time: "Julen nærmer sig" (Christmas is getting closer).

at nævne.explanation: "At nævne" means "to mention". It is related to "et navn" (a name), since you name something when you mention it. To say someone did not mention something, say: "Hun nævnte det ikke" (She did not mention it).

at nøjes med.explanation: "At nøjes med" means "to make do with". To say you accept a smaller option, put it after "med" (with): "Vi nøjes med en lille bil" (We make do with a small car).

at nøle.explanation: "At nøle" means "to hesitate". To say what you hesitate to do, add "med at" (with to) and the verb: "Han nølede med at svare" (He hesitated to answer).

en nabo.explanation: "En nabo" means "a neighbor". To talk about a woman next door, use the same word as for a man: "Min nabo er en sød dame" (My neighbor is a nice lady).

en nakke.explanation: "En nakke" means "a nape". To say the back of your neck hurts, say: "Jeg har ondt i nakken" (My nape hurts). Do not mix it up with "en hals" (a neck or throat): "Jeg har ondt i halsen" (I have a sore throat).

en narkoman.explanation: "En narkoman" means "a drug addict". A similar word is "en stofmisbruger" (a drug abuser): "Han er stofmisbruger" (He is a drug abuser).

en nat.explanation: "En nat" means "a night". To say at night, use "om natten" (at night): "Jeg sover om natten" (I sleep at night). To say tonight, use "i nat" (tonight): "Jeg sover hos dig i nat" (I am sleeping at your place tonight). To wish someone a good night, say: "Godnat, sov godt" (Good night, sleep well).

en nation.explanation: "En nation" means "a nation". To say the United Nations in full, use the plural: "De Forenede Nationer" (the United Nations). Its short form is "FN".

en nationalbank.explanation: "En nationalbank" means "a central bank". It is built from "national" (national) and "en bank" (a bank). In Denmark the central bank is called "Danmarks Nationalbank".

en nationalitet.explanation: "En nationalitet" means "a nationality". To ask someone, say: "Hvilken nationalitet har du?" (What nationality are you?) To answer, say: "Jeg er dansk" (I am Danish).
